title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
dek: Cash use keeps falling, yet currency in circulation keeps hitting records. Central banks have every incentive to keep printing $100 bills: the money is effectively a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, and the price is convenience for money launderers worldwide.
why: It strips money laundering back from "bank wires" to watches, tractors, casino chips and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks can't bear to kill the $100 bill.
who: Bank compliance, cross-border payments and monetary policy people, plus anyone curious about why banning the $100 bill is so hard.
skip: The first ~4 minutes are a live-event ad and small talk; jump straight to 5:09.

points.h: The scale of money laundering hasn't moved in thirty years
points.body: The most commonly used estimate of money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP a year, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP is $2 trillion to $5 trillion. That figure comes from a rough estimate by former IMF managing director Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and nobody has come up with a better answer since. Oliver warns that the more alarming fact is that the ratio hasn't changed in thirty years: decades of anti-money-laundering action have not shrunk the criminal economy, only barely held it from growing faster than the overall economy.

points.h: Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML for near-zero effect
points.body: When banks complain that KYC is too expensive, it isn't just whining. The U.S. passed the Bank Secrecy Act in 1970, and in 1989 the FATF turned anti-money-laundering into a global norm, forcing banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year — enough to solve world hunger and give everyone clean water. Yet the system generates enormous numbers of suspicious activity reports every year, and launderers still run ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is expensive, weakly fed back, and almost nobody is accountable for outcomes.

points.h: Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
points.body: Cash smuggling makes money laundering inside the banking system look small, but the bigger chunk never touches money at all: value is hidden in goods. Roughly $25 billion in cash flows into Mexico each year, while John Deere and Caterpillar farm equipment exported from the U.S. becomes the consideration cartels get back; European luxury goods flow to China, drugs and goods are imported back toward China, and the triangle is settled with misinvoiced paperwork. Global Financial Integrity estimates this kind of trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch on your wrist through customs is far easier than moving a million in cash.

points.h: The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets traffickers' supply
points.body: Each person in China has only a $50,000 annual foreign-exchange quota, while wealthy Chinese have plenty of demand to spend abroad. The Vancouver model matches that demand with drug cartels' supply of U.S. dollar cash: bags of cash outside Canadian casinos are handed to Chinese gamblers, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers owe a gambling debt; that debt is offset on the other end in China by an RMB transaction and by drug sales that follow. Looked at as a single gambling session it looks like a loss; looked at across the whole chain, it is a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates the traffickers' money and moves Chinese capital out. The model later spread worldwide, with luxury goods, consumer goods and drugs all serving as vehicles for moving value.

points.h: A VAT loophole lets the same goods extract 20% over and over
points.body: Zero-rated cross-border transactions in the EU were meant to keep national tax authorities from having to audit each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland owe no VAT, and when sold to a linked shell company 20% is added; that shell company then re-exports the goods to Ireland and claims back from UK tax authorities the 20% it never paid. Round and round it goes, hence carousel fraud. The UK once largely suppressed it with a multi-agency crackdown, and the fraudsters then moved to continental Europe, where it now runs about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania all the way to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no ceiling on cooperation: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

points.h: Nobody uses cash, yet central banks are printing record notes
points.body: In the age of digital payments, cash transactions are down to about 9% in the UK and about 13% in the U.S., so by ordinary logic the supply of paper money should be shrinking. After Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey raised the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon only intensified: the value of UK notes in circulation doubled, and the U.S. is near $2.5 trillion. Central banks blaming it on "store of value" doesn't hold up — surveys show the average American adult has only a bit over $400 on them, while per-capita U.S. currency in circulation works out to more than $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. bills are abroad, but that only pushes the question past the border: nobody knows whose hands these notes are actually in.

points.h: The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
points.body: Seigniorage can't simply be understood as the profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents, but it isn't "sold" to you — you can exchange it back for goods at face value at any time, so the cash the public holds is essentially an interest-free loan. With close to $2.5 trillion of U.S. currency in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funding equal to about 6% of the national debt; federal interest payments are now about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion also had to pay interest, you'd add roughly another percentage point. That is exactly why central banks don't want to hear anyone discuss abolishing cash.

points.h: AML incentives are inverted: the more reports, the less crime gets policed
points.body: Suspicious activity reports were born to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the exact opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to fill out reports, law enforcement has no resources to read them, and most reports go into a black hole; a bank that misses one can face billion-dollar fines, while getting it right earns no reward. A side effect is debanking — large numbers of people who come under suspicion, many of them Muslim, get cut off from financial institutions. The guest's solution isn't to hire more compliance officers but to generate fewer reports, actually read them, and genuinely prosecute financial criminals — raising the cost of money laundering instead of drowning everyone in paperwork.

quotes.text: But the most widely used estimate is that We're talking about between 2% and 5% of global GDP. And since global GDP is approximately $ 100 trillion, that means between $ 2 and $ 5 trillion being laundered globally.

Cash is a hugely significant tool for moving illicit wealth around the world. And even that is dwarfed by what we refer to as trade-based money laundering. It is essentially a way of moving value around the world, not in the form of money at all, but in the form of stuff.

So there is very little demand for cash from society. So you would expect, therefore, the supply of cash to be collapsing. And yet at the same time that the demand is very low, For some reason, supply is very, very high and getting higher all the time, consistently, almost everywhere.

if you take a $ 100 bill out the bank, you're not actually buying that $ 100 bill because you can sell it back at any time for the same amount that you bought it for. So actually, it's an interest-free loan to the government is what it really is.
if the US stops producing its $ 100 bill, and I wish it would, I don't think that there is anyone really, who would be inconvenienced by the lack of $ 100 bills except the bad guys.

Criminals have always liked to stack different techniques on top of each other. And so, yeah, cash remains the most useful criminal tool at a street level. But it's bulky, it's not secure. It's kind of annoying and smelly. It's annoying to count and so on. So if you can get away from using that as quickly as possible in order to move it around the world, that's where crypto comes in and is super useful.

Instead, we have a system that piles a huge amount of paperwork on financial institutions and a huge amount of expense and occasionally fines them for their trouble, but doesn't really do anything to stop financial crime. And that's kind of, as we say in Britain, ass backwards.
